newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says salmon threatened in northern California.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says salmon threatened in northern California.

text.p: In a long-awaited decision, the Clinton administration Friday declared coastal coho salmon a threatened species in northern California but not in most of Oregon.

The ruling under the Endangered Species Act, originally expected before last year's election, could limit activities such as logging, mining and road development up to 150 miles inland from the northern California coast.

The decision by the National Marine Fisheries Service was a victory for Oregon state officials, who had lobbied hard to win acceptance of their alternative plan to protect the species, a symbol of the Pacific Northwest that has been battered by decades of degradation to its natural habitat.
"I am confident that as a state and as a community, Oregonians can do the best job of restoring coastal coho salmon," Oregon's Democratic Governor, John Kitzhaber, said in a statement.

Environmental groups in both California and Oregon criticized the administration's decision, saying it did little to protect the species, which has dwindled to less than 10 percent of its population in the region just 20 years ago.

"The Clinton-Gore administration has made a political deal to accommodate the timber industry," said Ken Rait, conservation director of the Oregon Natural Resources Council, which is considering a legal challenge to the ruling.

After more than two years of study, the fisheries service listed coho salmon as threatened in a coastal territory that stretches from Punta Gorda, about 200 miles north of San Francisco, north to about 60 miles into Oregon at Cape Blanco.
William Stelle, head of the agency's Northwest regional office, said the population of the so-called "transboundary" coho group had fallen to less than 10,000 from as many as 400,000 historically.

But coho were merely listed as a "candidate" species for the Oregon territory from Cape Blanco north to the Columbia River, which includes about 80,000 fish currently, down from about 1 million in the late 1970s.

"In our judgment the biology does not indicate that they are at risk of extinction if we implement those components of the Oregon plan that are going to reduce substantially the risks to those stocks," Stelle said at a news conference.
Doug Wheeler, California's secretary for resources, said the state was "greatly disappointed" with the decision by the fisheries service to list the coho salmon in northern California.

"We remain confident that the state can reach agreement with the federal government and the affected interests on a formal agreement to protect the coho and other species of anadromous fish," he said in a statement.

U.S. Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat, said she supported the listing. "The sad facts on the diminishment of coho salmon and the destruction of the habitat it needs to survive are overwhelmingly persuasive in my view," she said.

Ray Wilkeson, legislative director of the Oregon Forest Industries Council, said timber companies were "very pleased" with the decision. "We really do believe ... that the fish are much better off with this decision than if it had gone the other way," he said.

"Today's decision basically says there's more than one way to save a species," Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden said in a statement. "Oregon has come up with a homegrown approach that brings people from all sectors together to work to recover our coho salmon runs."
